beats.intro: Module six. [[sub]]How to price a bond from its yield, and what moves the price.
beats.dcf: A bond's price is the present value of its promised cash flows. [[cf]]Take the five year bond with a three point two percent coupon, paid every six months. Each coupon is one point six, and the last payment adds the face value of one hundred. [[disc]]Discount each cash flow at the market discount rate. Suppose it is two percent every six months. [[pv]]Each payment is worth less today, and the later ones are worth the least. [[sum]]Add them up, and the price is ninety six point four one.
beats.premium: Compare the coupon rate with the market discount rate. [[disc]]When the market rate is above the coupon, the bond pays too little. Its price falls below par. It trades at a discount. At two percent every six months, ninety six point four one. [[par]]When the two are equal, the price is par, one hundred. [[prem]]When the market rate is below the coupon, the bond pays more than new bonds. Its price rises above par. It trades at a premium. At one point two percent every six months, one hundred three point seven five. [[end]]A rising market discount rate pushes the price down. A falling rate pushes it up.
beats.ytm: If the price is known, we can solve for the yield to maturity. [[def]]It is the single rate that makes the present value of the cash flows equal to the price. [[ex]]Say the same bond trades at one hundred eight point one five. [[solve]]Try different rates until the present value matches. The answer is about point seven five percent every six months, or one point five percent a year. [[assume]]The yield is your return only if you hold to maturity, the issuer pays in full and on time, and you reinvest the coupons at that same yield. [[neg]]Yields can even be negative, for example for zero-coupon bonds priced above par.
beats.flat: A bond often trades between coupon dates. [[acc]]Then the buyer owes the seller the interest earned so far, called accrued interest. [[saw]]The full price, also called the dirty price, rises each day as interest accrues, and drops when a coupon is paid. [[flat]]Dealers quote the flat price, the clean price, without accrued interest, so quotes do not jump. [[ex]]Take a bond with a one point five percent annual coupon, paid on June thirtieth and December thirty first, and a required yield of one percent every six months. Sixty days have passed out of one hundred eighty four. The full price is ninety nine point five eight seven. Accrued interest is point seven five times sixty over one hundred eighty four. That is point two four five. [[res]]The flat price is ninety nine point three four three.
beats.features: Price sensitivity depends on the bond's features. [[mat]]The longer the maturity, the bigger the percentage price change, for the same change in yield. A one point drop in yield lifts a five year bond a few percent, and a thirty year bond much more. [[cpn]]The lower the coupon, the bigger the percentage price change. A one percent coupon moves more than a six percent coupon. [[sym]]And for the same size move, a fall in yield raises the price by more than a rise in yield lowers it.
beats.matrix: Many bonds hardly trade. [[prob]]To price one, use matrix pricing. [[comp]]Find liquid bonds with similar credit quality and maturity, whose yields are known. [[interp]]Estimate the bond's yield, for example by interpolating between a three year and a five year bond. [[price]]Then discount the bond's cash flows at that estimated yield, to get its price. Matrix pricing is widely used for price quotes.
beats.wrap: Let's recap. [[w1]]Price is the present value of cash flows at the market discount rate. [[w2]]A coupon below the discount rate means a discount. Above it means a premium. [[w3]]Yield to maturity is the rate that makes present value equal to price. [[w4]]The quoted price excludes accrued interest, and long, low-coupon bonds swing the most.
